---
title: "Early-Pandemic Migration-Demand Shocks and Subsequent Rent Growth"
author: "Draft"
date: "May 2026"
format: pdf

# Abstract

This paper studies whether counties exposed to unusually large early-pandemic migration-demand shocks experienced faster subsequent rent growth. I define a county's migration shock as its 2021 IRS net migration rate relative to its own 2019-2020 pre-pandemic baseline and classify counties into five shock quintiles. The main empirical design uses a lagged binned difference-in-differences and event-study framework with county and year fixed effects, where post-treatment rent growth begins in 2022. This design treats migration as a broad demand shock rather than as a clean instrument for population growth.

# Design

The outcome is annual log rent growth from county-level ZORI. The treatment is:

$$
Shock_c = NetMigRate_{c,2021} - 0.5(NetMigRate_{c,2019}+NetMigRate_{c,2020}).
$$

Counties are divided into five quintiles of this early-pandemic abnormal migration shock. Q3 is the omitted middle-shock group, and the post period is 2022-2023.

The main DiD specification is:

$$
\Delta \log Rent_{ct}
= \sum_{q \in \{Q1,Q2,Q4,Q5\}}\beta_q Q_{cq}\times Post_t
+\alpha_c+\delta_t+\epsilon_{ct}.
$$

The event-study compares Q5 counties with Q3 counties, omitting 2019.

# Identification

The key identifying assumption is parallel trends: absent the early-pandemic migration-demand shock, high-shock and middle-shock counties would have followed similar rent-growth trajectories after 2021. The design uses early migration shocks, subsequent rent growth, county fixed effects, year fixed effects, and event-study pre-trend checks. The estimates are reduced form and should not be interpreted as the pure causal effect of population growth.

# Conclusion

The revised lagged five-bin design provides suggestive but not definitive evidence. The Q5 post coefficient is positive but imprecise, the event study shows a short-run 2022 increase followed by a 2023 reversal, and the low-permit heterogeneity estimate is not conclusive.
